body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Point-of-care lactate for identifying sepsis with organ dysfunction at emergency department triage: a pooled analysis of accuracy studies","authors":"Adeyemi-Lund S, Kowalczyk-Obi R, Tanaka-Brennan M","year":2021,"venue":"Rookhurst Emergency Care Reviews","doi":"10.5555/recr.2021.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We pooled accuracy studies of point-of-care lactate measured at emergency department triage in adults with suspected infection. At a threshold of 2 mmol/L, pooled sensitivity for sepsis with organ dysfunction was 0.65 and pooled specificity was 0.72 across 14 studies. At 4 mmol/L, sensitivity fell to 0.31 and specificity rose to 0.94. Heterogeneity was substantial, and studies that tested only patients who looked unwell reported higher sensitivity. Most studies defined sepsis from the hospital record without blinding to the lactate result. Point-of-care lactate alone misses a large share of patients with sepsis and should not be used to rule it out."},{"title":"Lactate and in-hospital mortality among adults with suspected infection in the emergency department: a review of observational studies","authors":"Mensah-Harlow D, Lindqvist-Oduya P","year":2019,"venue":"Vellmar Critical Care Syntheses","doi":"10.5555/vccs.2019.0233","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed observational studies of adults with suspected infection in emergency departments that reported in-hospital mortality by initial lactate. In 22 studies, a lactate of 4 mmol/L or more was associated with higher in-hospital mortality than a lactate below 2 mmol/L, with unadjusted odds ratios between 2.1 and 6.8. Venous, arterial and capillary measurements were combined, and few studies measured lactate at triage rather than after medical assessment. Mortality among patients with lactate below 2 mmol/L was not negligible in the larger studies. The review supports lactate as a marker of risk but not as a triage rule on its own."},{"title":"Agreement between capillary and venous lactate in adults: a review of method comparison studies","authors":"Rutherford-Ansah K, Varga-Solberg L","year":2020,"venue":"Harthill Laboratory Medicine Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 11 method comparison studies of capillary point-of-care and venous laboratory lactate in adults. Mean bias was small, with capillary values about 0.3 mmol/L higher, but the limits of agreement widened at higher values and in patients with poor peripheral perfusion. Agreement was worse when the finger was cold or when the first drop of blood was used. Most studies were small and recruited convenience samples in the emergency department. The authors conclude that capillary lactate is adequate for triage decisions near 2 mmol/L if the sampling technique is standardised, and less reliable at high values."},{"title":"Triage lactate within sepsis pathways and time to antibiotics: a review of before-after pathway studies","authors":"Olawale-Fischer J, Castellanos-Kim H, Duarte-Mbeki A","year":2023,"venue":"Rookhurst Emergency Care Reviews","doi":"10.5555/recr.2023.0141","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 17 before-after studies of emergency department sepsis pathways that included lactate at triage. Pathways using triage lactate reduced median time to antibiotics by 38 minutes, with no clear effect on mortality. Several studies reported more patients moved to resuscitation areas and longer waits for other patients, but none measured the effect on patients who were not suspected of sepsis. Pathways changed several things at once, so the contribution of lactate itself could not be separated. Most studies had high risk of bias from secular trends and changing definitions of sepsis."},{"title":"Normal lactate and false reassurance in suspected sepsis: a pooled analysis of negative predictive value","authors":"Petrov-Achebe N, Holmberg-Rao S","year":2024,"venue":"Vellmar Critical Care Syntheses","doi":"10.5555/vccs.2024.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We pooled data from studies that reported outcomes for adults with suspected sepsis whose first lactate in the emergency department was normal. Among patients with a lactate below 2 mmol/L, 9 percent had sepsis with organ dysfunction and 3 percent died in hospital. False reassurance was more common among older patients and among patients taking beta blockers. The negative predictive value depended strongly on the prevalence of sepsis in each study population. We conclude that a normal lactate should not lower the priority of a patient who meets other sepsis criteria."},{"title":"Overlap of primary studies in reviews of lactate for sepsis: a methodological assessment","authors":"Nakamura-Ellis G, Fernandes-Ayo T","year":2025,"venue":"Harthill Evidence Synthesis Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We identified 19 reviews of lactate for the diagnosis or prognosis of sepsis and built a citation matrix of their included primary studies. The corrected covered area was 18 percent, indicating very high overlap, and five primary studies appeared in more than ten reviews. Reviews that reached opposite conclusions often shared most of their primary studies but differed in outcome definitions and thresholds. Few reviews reported which lactate sample type was used. We recommend that umbrella reviews of this topic present a citation matrix and avoid counting the same primary evidence more than once."},{"title":"Confidence in reviews of sepsis biomarkers: an appraisal with a standard critical appraisal checklist","authors":"Brandt-Nwosu E, Silva-Hartmann O","year":2017,"venue":"Harthill Evidence Synthesis Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We appraised 34 reviews of sepsis biomarkers, including lactate, procalcitonin and white cell count, with a standard critical appraisal checklist for reviews. Most reviews of sepsis biomarkers were rated at critically low confidence, mainly because they lacked a registered protocol, did not assess risk of bias in included studies or did not account for it in their conclusions. Reviews of lactate were no better than reviews of other biomarkers. Only three reviews were rated at high confidence. The appraisal predates several recent reviews, and one appraiser rated each review with checking of a sample."},{"title":"Regional consensus statement on early recognition of sepsis in adult emergency departments","authors":"Regional Emergency Care Network sepsis working group","year":2022,"venue":"Regional Emergency Care Network statements","doi":"10.5555/recn.2022.0005","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A working group of emergency physicians, nurses and microbiologists reviewed published evidence and agreed recommendations for early recognition of sepsis in adult emergency departments. The statement recommends measuring lactate in adults with suspected infection who meet at least one physiological criterion, and treating a lactate of 4 mmol/L or more as a trigger for immediate senior review. It does not recommend using a normal lactate to lower priority. The group acknowledged that the evidence for lactate at triage came mainly from reviews of low confidence and that the recommendations were based partly on consensus."}]}
